feedback: If a child stops at 6:4, the 'can this go smaller?' indicator stays red — prompt: 'Is there a number that divides BOTH again?' Both parts still share a factor of 2, so divide again to reach 3:2.
If a child reads 3:2 as 3/2, point to the snapped whole: count ALL the parts (3+2=5); the denominator is the total five blocks, so boys are 3/5.
If the scaled bars change shape after an operation, that operation did not preserve the relationship — check whether both parts were divided by the SAME factor (subtracting a constant does not work).
activities.intendedInsight: Simplifying a ratio keeps the same 'for every' relationship with smaller numbers; simplest form means no common factor remains; and converting to a fraction uses the whole (a+b) as the denominator.
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 12:8 and simplify it by repeatedly choosing a number to divide BOTH parts by (e.g. ÷4 straight to 3:2, or ÷2 to 6:4 then ÷2 again).
Watch two scaled bars drawn beside the numbers: as 12:8 becomes 6:4 becomes 3:2, the bars keep the same shape/proportion, showing the relationship is preserved.

Use a 'can this go smaller?' indicator that stays red while a common factor greater than 1 still divides both parts and turns green only when none does, so 'simplest form' becomes a testable end-state.
Then snap the 3 and 2 blocks together into one whole of 5 and read off the part-to-whole fractions 3/5 and 2/5 from the total number of blocks.
For a decimal or fraction ratio (0.5:2, or 1/2:1/3), first apply a scale-up step (×2, ×10, or a common multiplier) to reach whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2), then simplify.
activities.title: Ratio simplifying bench with a shape-stays-the-same check

feedback: If 3/2 is chosen for the fraction of the whole, explain it compares the two parts, not part to whole; the denominator must be the total of the parts (5), so boys are 3/5.
If 2/5 is chosen for the fraction of the whole, note that 2/5 is the second part's share; the first part is 3 of the 5 equal parts in total, giving 3/5.
If 6:4 is left as the simplify answer, note both parts still divide by 2, so it is not yet simplest form.
If a match is wrong, check that both parts of the matched ratio divide down to the same pair of numbers (3 and 2).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent writing, simplifying and converting of ratios, with the common errors made explicit through the wrong-answer options offered.
learnerActions: Fill in the blanks to simplify: 12:8 = ☐:☐ (expecting 3:2 in simplest form).
Match several ratios (12:8, 6:4, 9:6) to their shared simplest form 3:2.

Choose what fraction of the whole the first part of 3:2 represents, from options including 3/5 (correct), 3/2 (the part-to-part comparison read as a fraction) and 2/5 (the other part's share of the whole).
activities.title: Scored practice set with targeted ratio errors

feedback: If the child declares a ratio finished too early, ask again whether a single number divides both parts.
If the child subtracts, show that 12:8 → 4:0 removes one quantity entirely and no longer describes the same situation.
activities.intendedInsight: Simplest form is reached only when no factor divides both parts, and simplifying must preserve the 'for every' relationship (divide, do not subtract).
learnerActions: Work through one ratio aloud with a prompt such as 'Can both numbers be divided again?' at each step until no common factor remains.
State why 4:0 (from subtracting) cannot be a valid simplification: it would mean 'no girls', which changes the relationship.
activities.title: Verbal coaching of the simplest-form check
